tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_render
tools.description: Show a finished HTML page (chart, table, diagram, collage, mockup) inline in this thread, above your final text reply; call it before writing that reply. The reader already sees the page, so the reply should not announce it, say where it is, or restate it: add only what the page doesn't say. Preview with html_preview first. T3 fits the frame to the page's height at each reader's width. A height below the page's contentHeight caps the frame there, and the rest scrolls inside it. Write one self-contained document with inline <style> and <script>. Local images written as absolute file paths (src="/abs/shot.png", CSS url(/abs/bg.webp), or a JS string) are inlined automatically; remote http(s) URLs, such as a CDN chart library, load as-is. The frame is borderless on the thread's background, as wide as the reply column (728px on desktop by default, wider if the reader widens chat, about 360px on phones), and its left edge lines up with your reply text. The page sits on the thread's own background, so by default leave html, body, and the outermost element with no background color. This overrides general style preferences such as a fixed black page background. Use a fluid width with no horizontal padding on the outermost element, and no outer card, border, or banner title: the page is part of your reply. If a box needs its own background (a mock of a specific screen, a panel that must stand apart), give it at least 16px of padding on every side and var(--radius) corners, so content never touches its edge. Give charts fixed pixel heights rather than heights that scale with width. Let content set the page's height. Avoid viewport-based heights such as 100vh or height:100% on html or body; the frame grows to fit the page, so they can make it grow again and again. T3 injects its active theme as CSS custom properties on :root, and they follow the user's theme and light/dark mode live: --background (page background, identical to the thread around the frame), --foreground, --muted, --muted-foreground, --card, --card-foreground, --popover, --popover-foreground, --secondary, --secondary-foreground, --border, --input, --ring, --primary, --primary-foreground (solid buttons), --accent, --accent-foreground (brand accent), --accent-surface, --accent-surface-foreground, --destructive, --destructive-foreground, --destructive-surface, --warning, --warning-foreground, --warning-surface, --success, --success-foreground, --info, --info-foreground, --code-background, --code-foreground, --chart-1 ... --chart-6 (categorical series for charts), --radius, --font-sans, --font-mono. The base stylesheet sets html background/color/font from these, body margin to 0, and hides the page's scrollbar; your own CSS overrides it.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__schedule_task
tools.description: Create persistent work in the app scheduler that runs even when no turn is active. Pass schedule as a STRUCTURED OBJECT, never JSON text. Timers: {type:'interval', everyMs:3600000} is hourly; {type:'fixed_time', timeOfDay:'09:00', weekdays:[1,2,3,4,5]} is weekday mornings; report the returned nextRunAt. Webhooks: {type:'webhook'} runs once per request to a generated URL. The run sees the request ONLY through prompt placeholders: {{body.path}} (e.g. {{body.action}}, {{body.release.tag_name}}), {{headers.name}}, {{query.name}}, {{body}}, or {{request}} (method, headers with credentials redacted, and body). For a sender that signs requests, first call request_secret so the user enters the secret privately (never ask for it in chat or invent one), then set signature with the returned secretRef, e.g. GitHub: {type:'webhook', signature:{header:'x-hub-signature-256', encoding:'hex', prefix:'sha256=', secretRef}}. The result's webhookUrl is the public URL to give the user; if it is absent, this environment has no T3 Connect managed tunnel, so tell the user to enable T3 Connect remote access rather than sharing a path. Omit projectId for this thread's project. In this thread's project, runs post into THIS thread by default (bindToCurrentThread=true), which suits an orchestrator that sees every trigger, delegates work, and can dedupe against what is in flight; use false only when the user wants a fresh top-level thread per run. Elsewhere each run launches a fresh thread. Provider, model, and runtime settings inherit from this thread, or from the project default when there is no calling thread.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_launch
tools.description: Create an ordinary TOP-LEVEL thread with an explicit workspace binding before its agent starts. Use this when the user requests independent work, a new thread, or a PR stack in its own worktree; use delegate_task for child subagents. Set workspaceStrategy to {type:"worktree",baseRef:"parent-branch",branch:"new-branch",startFromOrigin:false} for a new worktree based on local commits, or {type:"existing_worktree",worktreePath:"/absolute/path",branch:"existing-branch"} to use an existing checkout. For upstream commits, set startFromOrigin:true. Omitted workspaceStrategy means the project root, NOT the caller's worktree. Omit projectId/modelSelection/modes to inherit those settings from the calling thread; a caller outside a T3 thread must pass projectId and gets the project's default model. Set scratch:true instead of projectId for a thread without a project: it runs in a fresh folder of its own, outside any repository. Put the task in message. Do not ask the agent to create its own worktree via shell: that does not update the thread binding. Each call creates a new launch with no retry key; retain threadId and use t3_thread_read/t3_thread_wait to follow preparation. To link a thread for the user, write `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with the threadId exactly as returned, not URL-encoded; T3 Code shows the thread's current title. After errors or lost responses, inspect t3_thread_list before retrying. Attachments must be pending uploads. The new thread may not run with broader runtime or interaction modes than the caller: the calling T3 thread's own modes, or the permission mode an outside agent was approved with.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_send
tools.description: Send a message to any T3 thread in this environment. The target cannot have broader permission modes than the caller. Use delegate_task with the full review context and a new clientRequestId for independent review rounds. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, send to its childThreadId. After the original task completes, a requested follow-up creates a fresh task in that child thread and returns taskId; its completion notifies the parent, and the original result stays unchanged. mode='auto' starts an idle thread, steers a fully active turn, or queues behind a turn that is not yet steerable. Use queue for a separate follow-up turn, steer for an in-flight update, or restart to interrupt-and-restart the active turn. clientRequestId makes retries idempotent.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_worktree_handoff
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Move this agent thread into a new git worktree. To launch a separate agent already bound to a new or existing worktree, use t3_thread_launch with workspaceStrategy instead. Creates the worktree branch (optionally from origin), re-points the thread at the worktree, and by default runs the project's setup script there. Changing the workspace detaches the live provider session, so the current turn ends shortly after the handoff is recorded; call this as the last action of the turn. To keep working after the handoff, pass continuationPrompt with the remaining work: it is queued as the thread's next message and starts a new turn inside the worktree with the conversation preserved. Without it the thread stays idle until the next message. The worktree is not removed automatically when the thread is deleted. Fails if the thread is already attached to a worktree.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__watch_pull_request
tools.description: Have T3 Code watch an open pull request for this thread, linking it first if needed. T3 Code checks it every two minutes and wakes you with a message when a check fails, the required checks pass, someone else comments or reviews, or the branch starts to conflict with its base. Use this to monitor or babysit a pull request instead of polling, sleeping, or running a watcher. Only comments posted after this call wake you, so handle the existing ones first, then end your turn. A wake is news, not a merge decision: check readiness yourself before merging. While T3 Code watches, the thread stays in the user's Working list, not their inbox. When you hand the work back to the user, call unwatch_pull_request first so the thread returns to their inbox. Watching ends when the pull request merges or closes, when its thread settles or is archived, when T3 Code fails to read it 8 times in a row (a host rate limit only delays it), when the user stops this thread, or when you call unwatch_pull_request. Unsettle the thread before starting a new watch. A subagent cannot watch: its parent thread owns the pull request.

content.thinking:
I have enough context now, so it's time to produce the actual content: 8 room drafts with varying plant counts, 8 rubric drafts across topics, 8 rewrite cases reusing room material, 4 dossier drafts with intentional drifts, and the README.

To keep this manageable and reduce risk of errors, I'll write small Python generator scripts in /tmp that assemble the draft text into JSON, letting me validate word counts and substrings programmatically before producing the final output files. I'll keep drafts around 620-700 words each to stay safely within the 550-900 range, and plan out where plant mentions need to be placed in each one.

Starting with the room cases: an op-ed arguing for congestion pricing downtown, where I'll invent a fictional city ("Port Ellery") rather than a real one to avoid factual accuracy issues with the unsupported-claim plant, plus a personal essay about a father's shortwave radio with jargon like "QSL cards" as an audience-gap plant.

Next up are a travel essay about an old salt road with an invented factual error about salt history and a nice strong-passage line about the road forgetting the sea, a science explainer on the brain's glymphatic sleep-clearing system with jargon and an invented statistic, and a policy memo on a vacancy tax where the actual recommendation gets buried until paragraph five.

I'm continuing to plot out the remaining rooms: a book review with an invented sales figure and spoiler assumptions, a startup essay about vertical software companies that leans on survivorship bias, and a short-story excerpt with a confusing POV switch and underdeveloped character motivation.

For the fiction room, I want a factual-error plant that a scholar persona would catch, like a real-world detail about how a lighthouse actually works, and each draft needs at least one planted issue per persona type (angel, scholar, devil, editor). Then I'm sketching the rubric topics — starting with a four-day workweek essay contrasting a strong version with specific pilot numbers against a weak, generic version, followed by a composting topic.

The remaining topics are a council memo on Sunday library hours and a personal essay on winter sea swimming, each paired with a weak counterpart that's padded, hedging, and repetitive despite being fluent. For the rewrite phase, I'm distributing editor and other personas across eight cases at different intervention levels — sentence-level fixes for op-ed bloat, paragraph-level fixes for a salt-roads passage, and jargon cleanup for an explainer piece.

Continuing to map out rewrite cases, giving coverage to devil's advocate, scholar, and angel personas for the memo, review claim, story POV, and essay passages, making sure each preserves required verbatim substrings. Now I'm starting on the dossier section with four cases, beginning with one about register/audience targeting.

I'm now planning the implementation: splitting the builder into a few files per corpus, with a build script writing JSONL and a standalone validator reading it back. I'll keep all draft passages strictly ASCII—plain hyphens and straight quotes—and aim for 600-700 word drafts to satisfy the word-count targets, starting with the first draft now.

For draft one, I'm writing an op-ed on Port Ellery's downtown congestion charge, arguing that free driving at the point of decision is why decades of carrot-based fixes (widened approaches, underused bus lanes, half-empty park-and-rides) have failed, and that the council's upcoming vote should finally make drivers pay for the bridge.

I'm backing the case with evidence from Stockholm, London, and the fictional Verenport, each showing traffic drops and new revenue after similar charges took effect.

I need to address the regressivity objection head-on—yes, the fee hits a cleaner harder than a lawyer, but that cleaner is already likely riding the bus the charge would fund. I also want to dismiss the retail-decline fear as weak, noting that shoppers come for the stores, not the parking, and that the loudest opponents tend to be those with the biggest parking lots.

For the charge to survive politically, the money has to be transparently ring-fenced for transit, published and audited quarterly—exactly as the council's draft specifies—and members must resist any amendment that turns it into general revenue, since that would doom it. Success means a bridge that actually moves at rush hour, bus lanes with buses in them, and a park-and-ride shuttle that beats driving.

The council should pass the charge as written and give it three years before judging it—driving downtown will cost six dollars, and not driving will finally pay off, which is the whole bet worth making.

I'm also mapping out the piece's other hidden layers: an unsupported statistic to attribute to a scholar, a weak regressive-tax objection to voice as the devil's advocate, a bloated paragraph an editor would cut, and a standout passage describing what success actually looks like.

Then I start drafting a second piece, a personal essay called "The Shortwave," opening with a memory of a father's radio hissing with coded numbers broadcasts on the windowsill.

I continue the scene: he's not a spy but a self-taught tool-and-die maker with a secondhand Hallicrafters, logging distant stations and pinning QSL cards like a wall of unreachable places, while the teenage narrator treats the hobby as one more thing of his father's that doesn't belong to them.

After his death, clearing the back bedroom turns up eleven logbooks in his careful capitals, and one pencilled note, "Listened with Ruth," unlocks a memory his wife herself can't recall, suggesting grief surfaces unexpectedly through these small objects rather than the photographs he had braced for.

I bring the radio home, plug it in, and the hiss startles me as something that had felt like his alone, not the machine's. I turn the dial the way he taught me, and when a faint Spanish voice finally emerges from the static, I sit on the floor and write the time on an envelope, recognizing that he was never waiting for a message but simply listening to the world speaking into the dark, whether or not anyone heard it.

Now the radio sits ugly and glowing on my windowsill, mismatched with everything else, mostly hissing but occasionally catching something when the ionosphere obliges, and in those moments I lean in with a pencil and feel a little closer to understanding him. I'm noting some places in the piece that need grounding -- a line about QSL cards that a reader might not recognize, and an unsupported claim I should flag for support.

I'll skip that factual error and instead plant a weak-argument move: a line claiming unearned meaning, like "I do not know what I thought I was doing. I think that is the point," where the essay asserts significance it hasn't justified.

I'm also marking a strong passage about him listening to the world speaking whether or not anyone recorded it, and considering a bloat candidate describing the radio's ugly, dated appearance — though that image actually works well, so I may need another spot for bloat.

For the real bloat plant, I'll insert a flabby, self-indulgent sentence in paragraph three about being a self-absorbed teenager. For repetition, I'm weighing whether "the ionosphere was feeling generous" repeating twice should be a deliberate echo editors might flag, or whether I should instead plant a genuinely unintentional repeated phrase elsewhere to catch.

That settles the five plants for this draft — audience-gap, unsupported claim, weak argument, strong passage, and bloat. Now I'm moving to draft three, "Salt Roads," a travel essay about walking an old salt road from invented places like "Marrow Haven" to "Keld" along "the Salters' Way," roughly 38 miles across the moor, trying to keep the setting English-feeling without naming real locations.

I'm drafting the opening paragraphs: starting at Marrow Haven where the old salt pans are now a car park with a plaque that gets the history wrong, then tracing the packhorse route's four-hundred-year history from the monks at Keld Priory leasing the pans in 1312 to the railway ending the trade in the 1840s, noting flint and a Roman milestone along the way to suggest the path predates the salt trade itself.

I want to add the detail of sleeping the first night in an old barn by the milestone at Scarrow, and the shift from an abstract curiosity about what a road remembers into the simple physical need for the next stile. I'm also working out the logistics of the trade itself -- twenty-horse trains carrying roughly two tonnes of salt per run, leaving daily in season, moving more salt in a year than the county now consumes, all along a track easily lost in bracken.

The road's surface changes tell its own story: sunken hollow ways of sand over clay near the coast, a faint greener line marked by cairns across the peaty moor, and eventually a tarmac lane descending into the Keld valley until it becomes an ordinary street with a butcher's shop. Somewhere around the twelfth mile the sea itself disappears from view entirely, even though the salt, the horses, and the whole reason for the track all originated from that vanished coastline.

At Scarrow I met Doug, seventy-one, who claims to have walked this road over nine hundred times. He told me the moor's cairns are newer than they look -- his father built the largest one in 1952 after two walkers died in fog -- and when I asked what the road itself remembered, he gave me a look like I'd asked a sheep its opinion on scenery.

The thing about salt, I'm thinking in my sleep-deprived state, is that it leaves no trace -- it dissolves -- so the whole road becomes a record of something no longer there. In Keld, now a market town selling cheese and fudge instead of salt, I sat on the old weighing cross eating fudge and realized the road doesn't need to remember anything, since persisting is simply what roads do.

I'm checking the timeline against the scholar's claim: 1312 to the 1840s is actually over five hundred years, not four hundred, so that's a planted internal arithmetic error. Then there's the unsupported claim about the road carrying more salt annually than the whole county eats now, paired with pack-horse math that actually checks out -- twenty horses at two hundredweight each comes to roughly two tonnes, which is correct.

I'm also flagging bloat in the self-indulgent aside about sleep deprivation and stiles, a weak-argument spot where the essay asserts its conclusion about roads instead of remembering, and an audience-gap around jargon like "hollow way" or "hundredweight" that general readers might not know. That rounds out six planted issues for this draft.

Now I'm moving to the fourth draft: a science explainer titled "Why your brain needs the night shift" about the glymphatic system, aimed at general readers of a popular science outlet.

I'm drafting the opening — introducing the idea that the brain runs a nightly cleaning cycle only possible during sleep, framing the discovery as recent and puzzling since the brain lacks its own lymphatic vessels unlike the rest of the body, which clears cellular waste through a dedicated drainage network.

Then I recall the pivotal 2012 Rochester study: researchers tracked a fluorescent tracer in mice and found it flowed through brain tissue along arteries during sleep, clearing waste out along veins, while staying nearly motionless during wakefulness — leading them to name this the glymphatic system. I'm noting that the process is physical, not chemical, since brain cells shrink substantially during sleep to widen the spaces between them for fluid to flow through.

Beta-amyloid clearance is the key finding here — in mice, amyloid cleared roughly twice as fast during sleep, and in humans just one night of sleep deprivation measurably raises amyloid in the hippocampus, giving neurologists reason to worry about chronic short sleep as an Alzheimer's risk factor.

I should stay cautious though: mice aren't people, tracer studies are indirect, and human evidence mostly comes from imaging fluid rather than waste directly. The glymphatic system is almost certainly real in humans, but "sleep washes your brain" is more slogan than settled science—the plumbing exists, though how much disease it actually explains is still an open question tied to noradrenergic tone and AQP4 channel polarization in astrocytes.

Still, practical lessons hold up: sleeping on your side clears tracer better in mice than back or stomach sleeping, likely due to gravity and neck vein geometry, and protecting the first half of the night matters most since that's when deep sleep and peak flow occur. The system also weakens with age—older mice clear tracer at roughly a third the rate of young ones, tracking arterial stiffening, though this curve hasn't been confirmed in people yet.

What's genuinely strange is how sleep used to look like an absence, a pause where nothing interesting happened, when really it's a shift change—one crew clocks off, another comes in with mops, and all they need is an empty building.

Checking for plants: the amyloid-deprivation claim is actually real but uncited, so that's a different issue than invented. I should swap in something like "older mice clear tracer at a third the rate" as the unsupported claim, since the real figure is closer to a 40% decline. The dense jargon paragraph about noradrenergic tone and AQP4 polarization is a clear audience-gap moment, and the "shift change" line stands out as the strongest passage in the piece.

For the weak-argument tag, the line about arterial stiffening being "hard to avoid" as an inference despite no human data fits well. For bloat, I'm weighing a few options — the "discovery is barely a decade old" opener is only mildly padded, so I'm considering swapping in something wordier like a sentence about a problem remaining "simply a puzzle" for a long time, since that repetition is a better example of unnecessary padding.

Now moving to draft five, a policy memo for city councillors recommending a residential vacancy tax, I'm starting with the memo header format and an opening paragraph establishing the scale of unoccupied homes in the central wards, setting up a background section that will cover other cities' approaches and the council's options.

I'm filling out the background data: roughly 18,400 dwellings in the central wards, with utility consumption data showing 7.9 percent likely unoccupied, up from 5.1 percent, concentrated in newer buildings near the harbour. I'm connecting this to concrete costs like declining ground-floor retail occupancy and falling school enrolment to build the case for the committee.

Then I'm looking at comparative policy evidence from other cities—Vancouver's Empty Homes Tax, Melbourne's land tax, and especially Verenport's two percent levy, which cut likely-unoccupied units by 38 percent and funneled most revenue into affordable housing—since this precedent seems most relevant given the similarity to our market.

The committee's options narrow to three: continue monitoring with no action, pursue voluntary registry and matching measures, or introduce a levy on units left vacant more than six months a year with exemptions for probate, renovation, and medical absence. I'm recommending the third path, a two percent levy phased in starting at one percent in year one, with first-year revenue estimated between 11 and 14 million dollars before accounting for behavioral changes.

On objections, the levy properly targets owners holding property as a store of value rather than legitimate hardship cases, which the exemptions already cover. For enforcement, I'm proposing a self-declaration model with water-consumption data used to flag audits rather than determine liability directly, with two full-time audit staff sufficient for the first year.

I also want to flag that public attention on this issue has grown considerably, so the committee's handling of it will draw scrutiny. The levy's goals are modest—returning several hundred homes to use, funding new construction, and signaling the council's stance—but they're the only realistic options this year. I should make sure the recommendation itself, the two percent levy option, is clearly stated rather than buried in the later paragraphs.

I'm also noting the unsupported Verenport statistic about a 38 percent reduction in unoccupied units, which needs scholarly backing, and flagging the weak argument that dismisses "store of value" owners as obviously the levy's intended target—this assumes speculation rather than considering second-home owners or whether the levy changes behavior versus just raising revenue. There's also padding in the public-opinion sentence that could be tightened.

For the strong passage, I'm trimming it down to fit the 40-word limit: "It will not build a single home. What it will do is return several hundred existing homes to use within two years, fund the construction of others, and signal that the council regards a dwelling as something to live in."—confirming the word count fits.

Now I'm looking at another potential unsupported-claim entry: "School rolls in the central wards have fallen while enrolment elsewhere in the city has risen." This reads as a correlation that could be used as a weak devil's-advocate argument implying vacancy causes falling rolls.

I'm moving to Draft 6, a book review for an invented novel, "The Lamplighters' Union" by Ilse Marrow, aimed at literary magazine readers. I'm drafting an opening that plays with the gap between hype and reality—noting its fair buzz, pre-sale deals, and the publisher's inflated claim—before pivoting to describe it as a genuinely good book that loses its footing in the final forty pages.

I'm setting the scene in an unnamed 1890s port city resembling Trieste, right before electric light arrives, and sketching the guild of lamplighters negotiating their own obsolescence—focusing on Marrow's sensory detail about the work itself. I'm also introducing her central figure, Anzelm Vrana, the union secretary who avoids reading despite being literate, drawn into the talks for reasons still unfolding.

Marrow writes Vrana with a dignity that avoids sentimentality, especially in his restrained, almost missable acceptance of a job maintaining the very dynamos replacing him. The novel's strength lies in refusing to romanticize the lamplighters—they're skilled but tired and sometimes cruel, resisting a genuinely better technology—and in asking what's owed to people whose expertise has become obsolete without offering easy answers. I'm noting the prose is consistently excellent, but something falters in how the book ends.

The last forty pages betray the ambiguity so carefully built over three hundred, as Vrana's daughter suddenly delivers an anachronistic speech about progress that feels unearned and tells readers exactly what to feel—undoing the restraint the novel had maintained. This is especially odd given that Marrow's previous two books, "Tidewater" and "The Cartographer's Daughter," both demonstrated she knows how to end a novel well, which makes me suspect editorial pressure here with an eye toward wider distribution.

Still, the commercial success is staggering—four hundred thousand copies in a month, reportedly the fastest-selling literary debut in the publisher's history—though that figure speaks more to marketing than merit. I keep returning to Marrow's finest image: a lamplighter climbing a ladder at dusk to light a lamp that will be obsolete within the year, doing his job properly anyway, because the lamp itself doesn't know its fate.

Also considering the "three hundred pages" phrase repeated four times — editor would flag that. Then there's a genuinely strong passage about a man lighting a lamp at dusk, which deserves an angel tag, and an audience-gap issue around a speech about progress that doesn't fit the established timeframe, something a careful reader would catch as a minor inconsistency.

I'm testing a plant referencing her two earlier novels, "Tidewater" and "The Cartographer's Daughter," without clarifying they're her prior work until it's implied through context — that assumes the reader already knows, so it needs an expected-reader note. I think five plants should suffice, covering the weak-argument sentence, the repetition, the strong passage, the audience-gap, and this allusion issue.

Now I'm drafting a startup/industry essay titled "Why vertical software wins," aimed at founders and operators reading a newsletter — arguing that the next decade's biggest software companies will be narrow, industry-specific tools (for dentists, freight brokers, car washes) rather than horizontal platforms, because that's where the margin has shifted, and contrasting this against the old twenty-year-old wisdom of building general-purpose tools for every market.

I'm making the case that building software is no longer the hard part — understanding the customer is — using the freight broker example to show how vertical tools embed domain knowledge from day one, then citing Toast, ServiceTitan, and Procore as proof that vertical-focused companies have outcompeted horizontal incumbents in their industries.

The data I'm recalling shows vertical companies reaching $10M ARR about fourteen months faster than horizontal peers, with much stronger retention, because they can monetize the payment flow itself rather than just charging subscriptions for watching the money pass by. I'm anticipating the obvious counterargument about market size being too small.

The real issue isn't customer count but how much of each customer's revenue you can capture—a dental practice turning over a million dollars a year, taxed at a few percent across thousands of practices, dwarfs most horizontal businesses, especially since switching costs lock customers in. But the sharper critique is that this same vertical focus becomes a ceiling: a freight-brokerage tool thrives only within freight brokerage, and contracts along with that industry, whereas horizontal tools survive by being diversified. I think this critique is valid but doesn't overturn the overall conclusion.

There's also the honest concern that the vertical success stories cited are survivors, and there's likely a much longer, unwritten list of vertical companies that failed quietly. Still, the practical lesson holds: build from an industry you've actually worked in, solve its most hated workflow obsessively, then monetize the money flowing through it—that's what compounds, while generic tools hoping a vertical adopts them mostly get acquired for less than they raised. Software used to be scarce, but now customer knowledge is the scarce resource, which is exactly what the vertical company possesses.

I also want to flag two more distinct bloat passages in that same paragraph: the editor-style hedge "It is also worth saying, because people do say it, and it needs to be addressed, that there is a question about whether," and the weak-argument continuation about whether there's a longer list of vertical companies that didn't succeed.

Then there's a strong angel passage about knowledge of the customer being the form that takes shape when a company decides to charge rent, and a buried-lede issue where the real thesis—that vertical companies win because they can charge for the workflow plus take a cut of the money flowing through—doesn't surface until midway through. That gives me six plants total, including the buried-lede, which feels like enough. Now I'm moving on to Draft 8, a short-story excerpt.

I'm picturing "The Keeper's Daughter," a lighthouse story written in third person around a girl named Nell, with a deliberate POV slip into her father's perspective. She's been taught to count seconds between flashes using "Mississippi" as a beat, though she's skeptical the river even exists, and her father has explained that each lighthouse has its own rhythm, like a heartbeat, which sailors use to navigate in the dark. It's her first night in the lamp room at age nine, having promised to keep her hands off everything.

Now I'm following her sitting almost an hour, listening to the mercury-bath turning of the lamp behind her and her father winding the weight below, the chain's jerky ascent mixed with his breathing and the sea's sound, which she'd long stopped noticing until she had to remember it was there. Every weekday morning, roughly forty thousand cars cross the Harbour Bridge into downtown Port Ellery, and almost every one of them carries a single person. The city has spent two decades trying to fix this with carrots. It has widened the bridge approach twice, added a bus lane that is routinely full of cars, and built a park-and-ride that sits half empty because the bus from it takes longer than driving. None of this has worked, and the reason is simple: driving downtown is free at the moment of decision, and anything free at the moment of decision will be overused.

The council will vote next month on a downtown congestion charge of six dollars per weekday entry. It should pass it, and it should resist the temptation to water it down.

The case rests on a plain fact about behaviour. When something costs nothing at the point of use, people treat it as if it costs nothing at all, even when the road, the air and their own mornings are paying for it. A charge does not punish drivers. It asks them to see the price that was always there. That is the whole argument.

Cities that have tried this have not regretted it. When Stockholm introduced its charge, traffic into the centre fell by about a fifth and stayed down. London's charge cut congestion in its first year and funded a bus network that still carries the people the charge priced off the road. Closer to home, Verenport's cordon charge cut peak-hour crossings by 31 percent in eighteen months and raised 44 million dollars for transit, and Verenport is a city of almost exactly our size, with a harbour, a single bridge, and a downtown that used to be a car park at nine in the morning.

The main objection is that a charge is regressive: six dollars means more to a hospital cleaner than to a lawyer. This is true, and it is also beside the point, because the cleaner is far more likely to be on the bus already, and the bus is the thing the charge pays for.

A second objection says the charge will kill downtown retail. The evidence for this is thin. Shoppers do not come downtown because parking is pleasant; they come because the shops are there, and they will keep coming on a bus that runs on time. The retailers who have raised the alarm are, in my experience, mostly the ones with the largest car parks.

It is also worth remembering, and this cannot be stressed enough, that the problem we are dealing with here is one that affects everybody in this city, whether or not they personally own a car or drive one, and that the costs of doing nothing are costs that we are all already paying in one form or another, every single day, whether we notice them or not.

What the charge needs in order to work is honesty about where the money goes. Every dollar should be ring-fenced for the bus and ferry network, published quarterly, and audited. The council's draft does this. Members should not let it be amended into a general revenue measure, because the moment the charge looks like a tax, it will be fought like one.

Here is what success looks like. A bridge that moves at eight in the morning. A bus lane with buses in it. A park-and-ride whose shuttle is faster than the car it replaces. A downtown where a delivery van can find the kerb. None of these things is exotic. All of them exist in cities that decided the road was worth something.

The council should pass the charge, pass it whole, and give it three years before anyone is allowed to call it a failure. Driving downtown will cost six dollars. Not driving downtown will finally be worth something. That trade is the whole argument, and it is a good one.

My father kept a shortwave radio on the windowsill of the back bedroom, and for most of my childhood I thought it was broken. It hissed. Occasionally it produced a voice reading numbers in a language I did not know, and he would lean toward it with a pencil, writing on the back of an envelope, and then the voice would be gone and the hiss would come back and he would sit for a while longer as if the hiss itself were saying something.

He was not a spy. He was a tool-and-die maker who had taught himself Morse from a library book in 1961 and never found anyone to use it with. The radio was a Hallicrafters he had bought secondhand, and on good nights, when the ionosphere was feeling generous, it could pull in Radio Netherlands, the BBC World Service, a station in Quito that played the same four hymns, and a Soviet numbers station he called "the lady." He logged everything. He sent for QSL cards and pinned them above the desk, a wall of postmarks from places he would never go.

I understood none of it, and I did not try to. I was a teenager, and like most teenagers I was, if I am honest about it, mostly interested in myself and in the things that were happening to me at that particular moment in my life; the radio belonged to the same category as his fishing lures and his opinions about carburettors, things that were his and therefore not mine. The one time he tried to show me how to find a station by the sound of the carrier wave sharpening as you turned the dial, I said I had homework, and he said all right, and turned back to the hiss.

He died in March. In May I was clearing the back bedroom and found the logbooks, eleven of them, in his small square capitals. 14 Feb 1974. 0340 UTC. 9.410 MHz. BBC. Weak, fading. News of the miners. And under it, in pencil: Listened with Ruth. That was my mother. She has no memory of it. She says she must have fallen asleep in the chair.

Everyone who has lost a parent knows that grief arrives through objects, and that the objects are never the ones you expect. I had braced for the photographs. I had not braced for a column of frequencies, or for the discovery that my father had kept a record of the nights my mother sat up with him, as carefully as he kept the signal strength.

I took the radio home. I plugged it in and it hissed, which I had somehow not expected, as if the hiss had been his and not the machine's. I turned the dial the way he had shown me once, slowly, listening for the carrier to sharpen, and for a long time there was nothing, and then there was a voice in Spanish, very faint, and I sat down on the floor and wrote the time on the back of an envelope.

I do not know what I thought I was doing. I think that is the point. He did not know either, not in any way he could have told me. He was not waiting for a message. He was listening to the fact that the world was out there, speaking, whether or not anyone was writing it down, and he had decided that someone should.

The radio is on my windowsill now. It is an ugly object, brown and grey, the size of a bread bin, with a dial that glows a colour nobody has used since 1958. It does not match anything in the room. Most nights it just hisses. Sometimes, late, when the ionosphere is feeling generous, it finds something, and I lean toward it with a pencil, and I understand my father a little, and the hiss comes back, and I sit for a while longer.

The salt road starts where the sea used to be. At Marrow Haven the pans are a car park now, flat and white in the wrong way, and the only sign that anyone ever boiled brine here is a plaque the council put up in 1987, which gets the century wrong. I read it twice, decided not to care, and walked inland.

For four hundred years, from the time the monks at Keld Priory first leased the pans in 1312 until the railway killed the trade in the 1840s, packhorses carried salt along this track: thirty-eight miles from the coast to the market at Keld, two days with a load, three in rain. The route is older than the salt. Flint turns up along it, and a Roman milestone sits in the churchyard at Scarrow, which is where I slept the first night, in a barn that had been a barn when the milestone was new.

I had come to walk the road because I wanted to know what a road remembers. That is the kind of sentence you write before you set out. By the second morning, with my boots not yet dry and the moor opening ahead like a grey sea with the water taken out, I had stopped wanting to know anything and simply wanted the next stile.

The salters walked in trains of twenty horses, each horse carrying two hundredweight in panniers, which comes to roughly two tonnes of salt per train. A train left Marrow Haven every weekday in the season. At that rate the road carried more salt in a year than the whole county eats now, and it did it on a track you could lose in bracken.

The surface tells you where you are. Near the coast it is sand over clay, and the horses' feet have worn it into a hollow way three metres deep, so that you walk between walls of root and earth with the sky a strip overhead. Up on the moor it is peat and stone, and the road is a line of slightly greener grass, marked at intervals by cairns that someone still maintains. Coming down into the valley of the Keld it becomes a lane with a tarmac spine and grass shoulders, and then a road, and then a street with a butcher on it.

The road forgot the sea entirely somewhere around the twelfth mile. I kept looking back for it and there was only moor. The salt had come from there, and the horses had come from there, and the track had been made by nothing but their wanting to get away from it, and yet nothing about it now said sea. It said sheep. It said wind. It said, mostly, nothing, which is what moors say.

At Scarrow I met a man named Doug who has walked the road, by his count, over nine hundred times. He is seventy-one and does it in a day, there and back, when the weather is right, which he said it rarely is. He told me the cairns on the moor are not old at all; his father built the biggest one in 1952 after two walkers died in fog, and the one before that fell down in a storm nobody remembers. I asked him what the road remembered. He looked at me the way you would look at someone who had asked a sheep what it thought of the view.

The thing about a salt road, I want to say, and I say it knowing that it is the sort of thing a person says who has been walking for two days on not much sleep and has started to find significance in stiles, is that salt is the one cargo that does not leave a trace, because it dissolves, so that the whole road is a record of something that is no longer there.

Keld, when I got there, was having a market. Not a salt market; it sells cheese now, and candles, and a kind of fudge. I bought the fudge. I sat on the steps of the cross where the salt had been weighed and ate it and watched the town not remember anything at all, and it occurred to me that the road did not need to remember, because it was still there, which is what roads do instead.
""")

EXPLAINER = D("""
Every night, while you are doing nothing, your brain runs a cleaning cycle that it cannot run while you are awake. The discovery is barely a decade old, it has already changed how researchers think about sleep, and it begins with a question that sounds like a riddle: how does an organ with no lymphatic vessels take out its rubbish?

The rest of the body has a drainage network. Lymph vessels run alongside blood vessels, collecting the fluid and waste that leak out of cells and carrying it off to be filtered. The brain, which produces waste faster than almost any other tissue, has no such vessels inside it. For a century this was simply a puzzle, and it remained a puzzle for a long time, as puzzles tend to do when nobody has the tools to solve them. Neurons make junk, the junk goes somewhere, and nobody could say where.

In 2012 a group at the University of Rochester watched the answer happen in mice. They injected a fluorescent tracer into the cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid that bathes the brain, and watched where it went. During sleep the tracer poured into the brain along the outside of arteries, swept through the tissue, and left along the outside of veins, taking dissolved waste with it. During waking it barely moved. The team called the network the glymphatic system, after the glial cells that line its channels, and the name stuck.

The mechanism is mechanical rather than chemical. When you sleep, the cells of the brain shrink by around sixty percent, opening the spaces between them, and fluid can flow through tissue that was packed tight an hour earlier. The pulse of the arteries pushes it along. Slow-wave sleep, the deep stage that dominates the first half of the night, produces large, slow swells of blood flow, and each swell drives a wave of fluid through the tissue behind it.

What gets washed out matters. One of the waste products is beta-amyloid, the protein that clumps into the plaques found in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease. In the Rochester mice, amyloid cleared about twice as fast during sleep as during waking. In humans, a single night of sleep deprivation raises amyloid in the hippocampus by a measurable amount, which is one of the reasons neurologists have started to take chronic short sleep seriously as a risk factor rather than a lifestyle complaint.

It is important to be careful here. Mice are not people, tracer studies are indirect, and the human evidence comes mostly from imaging that measures the fluid rather than the waste. The glymphatic system is real in rodents and almost certainly real in us, but "sleep washes your brain" is a slogan, not yet a settled finding, and the honest version is that the plumbing exists and the question is how much of the disease it explains.

Clearance is modulated by noradrenergic tone, and the perivascular influx is sensitive to the AQP4 polarisation of astrocytic endfeet, which is why the knockout models showed such a striking reduction in tracer penetrance.

Still, the practical lessons are not controversial. Sleep on your side, if you can; in mice, lateral sleeping cleared tracer better than lying on the back or the front, and the reason seems to be gravity and the geometry of the veins in the neck. Protect the first half of the night, because that is when deep sleep happens and deep sleep is when the flow is strongest. Treat a week of five-hour nights as something you did to your brain, not merely something you felt.

The system also seems to weaken with age. Older mice clear tracer at roughly a third the rate of young ones, and the decline tracks the stiffening of arteries, which push less fluid with each pulse. Nobody has shown the same curve in people, but the stiffening of arteries with age is not in doubt, and the inference is hard to avoid.

Which leaves the thing that is genuinely strange about all this. For most of the history of biology, sleep looked like an absence, a period in which the interesting processes stopped. It turns out to be a shift change. The crew that runs the day clocks off, and a different crew comes in with the mops, and the only thing they ask is that the building be empty.
""")

MEMO = D("""
To: Housing and Planning Committee
From: Policy Analysis Unit
Re: Residential vacancy in the central wards

Over the past three years the committee has received a growing volume of correspondence about homes in the central wards that appear to be unoccupied for most of the year. This memo sets out what we know about the scale of the problem, reviews the approaches other cities have taken, and offers an assessment of the options available to the council.

Background. The central wards contain roughly 18,400 dwellings. Utility data obtained under the information-sharing agreement with Ellery Water indicates that 1,460 of these, or 7.9 percent, used less than ten percent of median household water consumption in each of the last four quarters, which is the threshold the agreement defines as "likely unoccupied." This figure has risen from 5.1 percent in the first year of the agreement. The increase is concentrated in buildings completed after 2019 and in the two wards closest to the harbour.

Unoccupied housing in these numbers has costs. Street-level retail depends on resident footfall, and the Harbour Ward business association reports vacancy among ground-floor units of 22 percent. School rolls in the central wards have fallen while enrolment elsewhere in the city has risen. Units held empty are units not available to the 3,100 households currently on the council's housing register.

Other cities. Vancouver introduced an Empty Homes Tax in 2017 at one percent of assessed value, later raised to three percent; the city reports that the number of vacant properties fell by more than half over four years, though some of that decline reflects owners reclassifying properties rather than letting them. Melbourne's vacant residential land tax applies at one percent and has been criticised as too low to change behaviour. Verenport, whose housing market most closely resembles ours, adopted a two percent levy in 2021 and recorded a 38 percent reduction in likely-unoccupied units within two years, with 61 percent of the revenue directed to its affordable housing fund.

We should note that the evidence base is small, that cities differ in enforcement capacity, and that the Vancouver data in particular has been contested by the development industry.

Options. The committee has, broadly, three choices. It can take no action and continue monitoring. It can pursue voluntary measures, such as a registry of long-term vacant units and a matching service connecting owners with the housing register. Or it can introduce a levy on dwellings unoccupied for more than six months in a year, with exemptions for probate, renovation, and medical absence.

Our recommendation is that the committee adopt the third option, a levy of two percent of assessed value, phased in over two years, with the first year at one percent. We estimate first-year revenue at 11 to 14 million dollars before behavioural response, declining as owners let or sell. We recommend that the revenue be ring-fenced for the housing fund.

The main argument against a levy is that it is a tax on ownership rather than on harm, and that owners have legitimate reasons for leaving a property empty. The exemptions address this. The remaining cases, owners who hold property empty as a store of value, are exactly the cases the levy is meant to reach, and it is difficult to see why the council should protect them.

A second concern is enforcement. The water-consumption method produces an indicator, not a determination, and some owners will dispute it. We propose a self-declaration model, as in Vancouver, with the water data used to target audits rather than to assess liability directly. Audit capacity of two full-time staff should be sufficient in the first year.

It should also be said, and it is worth the committee bearing this in mind as it considers the matter, that this is a question on which public opinion in the city has, over the period in question, become considerably more engaged than it was previously, and that the committee's handling of it will be watched with some interest.

The levy will not solve the housing shortage. It will not build a single home. What it will do is return several hundred existing homes to use within two years, fund the construction of others, and signal that the council regards a dwelling as something to live in. These are modest goals. They are also the only ones available to the committee this year.
""")

REVIEW = D("""
Ilse Marrow's third novel arrives with the kind of reputation that usually precedes a disappointment. "The Lamplighters' Union" was the most talked-about manuscript at last year's Frankfurt fair, sold in twenty-six territories before a single reviewer had read it, and has been described by its publisher, with a straight face, as "the novel of the decade." It is not that. It is something rarer and more useful: a good book that knows exactly what it is doing for three hundred pages and then, for forty more, forgets.

The setting is a port city in the 1890s, unnamed but recognisably Trieste, in the last years before electric light. The lamplighters of the title are a guild of about two hundred men who walk the streets at dusk with their poles and ladders, and the plot, such as it is, follows the guild's doomed attempt to negotiate its own obsolescence. Marrow is wonderful on the texture of the work: the smell of the oil, the particular ache of a shoulder that has carried a ladder for thirty years, the way a lamplighter learns a city by its corners and comes to resent any street that has been straightened.

Her hero, if the word applies, is Anzelm Vrana, the union's secretary, a man who can read but prefers not to, and who is drawn into the negotiations because he is the only one who can be trusted not to want anything. Marrow gives him a dignity that never tips into sentiment. When he is finally offered a job with the electric company, maintaining the dynamos that will replace him, the scene is written with such restraint that the reader has to go back to find the moment he says yes.

The book's great achievement is its refusal to make the lamplighters right. They are not noble. They are skilled, tired, frightened and occasionally cruel, and the electric light they are resisting is, as Marrow never lets us forget, better. The novel asks what is owed to people who were good at something the world no longer needs, and it has the honesty not to answer.

The prose is excellent throughout, really excellent, and Marrow's sentences are consistently well made.

What goes wrong is the ending. Having spent three hundred pages earning her ambiguity, Marrow spends the last forty resolving it. Vrana's daughter, who has been a minor presence, suddenly becomes the novel's moral centre and delivers a speech about progress that nobody in 1894 would have given and that the book has not prepared us to hear. The lamps go out. The city is lit. The reader is told what to feel about it, which is precisely what the preceding chapters had so carefully declined to do.

It is a strange failure of nerve from a writer who has shown, twice before, that she can end a book. "Tidewater" closed on a single sentence of dialogue. "The Cartographer's Daughter" simply stopped. Here, one suspects an editor with an eye on the twenty-six territories.

Readers who loved "Tidewater" will find the same cold intelligence here, and the same gift for the material life of work. Readers coming to Marrow for the first time should start with this one anyway; the first three hundred pages are as good as anything published this year, and the daughter's speech can be skipped.

The novel has already sold over four hundred thousand copies in its first month and is said to be the fastest-selling literary debut in its publisher's history, a figure that tells you something about the publicity and nothing about the book.

Whether it lasts is a different question. The lamplighters, in the end, did not, and Marrow knows it. Her best pages are the ones in which a man climbs a ladder in the dusk to light a lamp that will be gone in a year, and does it properly, because the lamp does not know.
""")

STARTUP = D("""
The best software companies of the next decade will not be built for everyone. They will be built for dentists, or freight brokers, or the people who run car washes, and they will be worth more than the horizontal tools they replace. This is not a prediction about niches. It is a prediction about where the margin went.

For twenty years the standard advice was to build the general tool. Make the spreadsheet, the CRM, the project tracker, and let every industry adapt it. The logic was that a big market beats a small one, and that a tool used by every company would be worth more than a tool used by one kind. The logic was right as long as the hard part was building the software. It is no longer the hard part.

What is hard now is knowing the customer. A freight broker does not want a CRM. She wants to know which of her forty carriers will actually show up on Thursday, and she wants the software to already know that a load from Harrowfield to the port needs a tarp and a driver with a hazmat endorsement. The general tool can be configured to do this, by someone, eventually. The vertical tool does it on the first day, because the people who built it used to be freight brokers.

Look at the companies that have actually compounded. Toast started as a restaurant point-of-sale and became the restaurant's bank. ServiceTitan sells to plumbers and is worth more than most of the horizontal tools its customers used to patch together. Procore owns construction. In each case the company began by solving one workflow completely and then found that the customer, having trusted it with the workflow, would trust it with the payments, the payroll, the lending and the insurance.

Our analysis of the 212 vertical software companies that raised a Series A between 2015 and 2020 found that they reached 10 million dollars in annual recurring revenue a median of fourteen months faster than horizontal companies in the same cohort, and that their gross retention at year three averaged 94 percent against 81.

This is why the vertical company wins. It can charge for the workflow and then take a percentage of the money that flows through it. The horizontal tool charges a subscription and watches the money go past.

The objection is obvious: the market is small. There are only so many dentists. But the number that matters is not the count of customers; it is the share of each customer's revenue you can touch. A dental practice turns over around a million dollars a year. Touch three percent of that across ten thousand practices and you have a business larger than most horizontal tools will ever be, selling to people who will never leave because leaving means re-entering their patients' records by hand.

The counterargument that matters more is the one people do not raise: that the vertical company's moat is also its ceiling. The freight-broker tool is wonderful at freight brokerage and useless for anything else, and when the industry contracts, as freight does every few years, the software contracts with it. The horizontal tool is dull but it is diversified.

I think this is a fair point and that it does not change the conclusion.

It is also worth saying, because people do say it, and it needs to be addressed, that there is a question about whether the examples that get cited in essays like this one are the examples that happened to work, and whether there is a longer list, somewhere, of vertical companies that did not, and that nobody writes essays about.

The practical advice, then. If you are starting a company, pick an industry you have worked in, not one you have read about. Find the workflow its people hate most and do that one thing until it is boring. Then, and only then, go after the money that moves through it. The companies that did this are the ones that compounded. The companies that built a general tool and hoped a vertical would adopt it are, mostly, the ones that got acquired for less than they raised.

The general tool was the right answer when software was scarce. Software is no longer scarce. Knowledge of the customer is, and the vertical company is simply the form that knowledge takes when it decides to charge rent.
""")

STORY = D("""
Nell had been told to count the seconds between the flashes, and she counted them the way she had been taught, with a "Mississippi" after each number, though she had never seen the Mississippi and privately doubted it existed. Four. The light swung round and went out over the water and came back. Four again. Her father said that was how a sailor knew which light he was looking at, because every lighthouse in the world had its own time, like a heartbeat, and a sailor who knew the heartbeats could tell where he was in the dark from forty miles out.

She was nine. It was the first night he had let her sit up in the lamp room, and she had promised not to touch anything, and she had kept the promise for almost an hour.

The lamp itself was behind her, inside its glass, turning on its bath of mercury with a sound like a very slow clock. Her father was below, winding the weight. She could hear the chain going up through the tower in jerks, and his breath between the jerks, and under that the sea, which was the sound she had stopped hearing years ago and had to remember to listen for, the way you have to remember to notice that you are breathing.

Out on the water there was a ship. She saw its lights first, red and green, and then the dark shape between them, and she counted it as she counted everything: a ship, one Mississippi, still there. It was closer than ships usually came. Her father had said the rocks ran out a mile from the point and that was why the light was here, to tell the ships about the rocks, and this ship did not seem to have been told.

She should have called down. She knew that. She thought of the chain going up and her father's breath, and she thought that if she called down he would come up and look and say it was nothing, a fishing boat, and then he would not let her sit up again, and so she watched the ship instead, and counted, and the light went round.

Thomas, winding the weight, had been thinking about the girl's mother, which he did most nights at about this hour, when the work was mechanical and the mind went where it wanted. He did not hear the ship. He did not hear anything but the chain. He was thinking that the girl had her mother's way of looking at a thing as if it owed her an explanation, and that it would get her into trouble, and that he would not be there for all of it.

The ship's green light went out. Nell waited for it to come back and it did not, and she understood, in the slow way that a child understands things that are too large, that the ship had turned, and that the side of it she could see now was the side with no light on it, and that it was turning toward the rocks.

She went to the top of the stairs. She did not call. She stood at the top of the stairs with her hand on the rail, which was cold, and which she was not supposed to touch, and she looked down into the dark of the tower and listened to the chain, and she thought very clearly, and in words, for the first time in her life: if I say nothing, this is mine.

The sea was very calm that night, calmer than it had been for a month, and the sky was clear and there was no wind at all, and the stars were out over the water in their thousands, and the whole of the bay lay under them as still as a plate, and the ship went on turning.

Below her, the chain stopped. Her father's breath stopped with it, and then there was his voice, coming up the tower, saying her name, not loudly, the way he said it when he already knew something was wrong. She did not answer. The light went round. Four Mississippi. The ship had no lights at all now, and she could not see it, and she could not stop seeing it.
""")
